_comment: The Quiz bank: short hand-written questions an IOAI contestant can answer from ML knowledge, no arithmetic. Four options, one right (answer = its index), a one-line why shown after. pack = the topic a live topic match deals it under; lvl = easy or medium. data/daily.json `quiz` lists the Daily Quiz's hand-picked days. rq-01..rq-80 are the first bank, retired (never dealt, kept so old results still open). Ids are stable: never renumber.

questions.q: Training loss keeps falling, but validation loss has started to rise. What is happening?
options: The model is overfitting the training data
The learning rate is too small to make progress
The model is underfitting and needs more epochs
The validation set has leaked into training
questions.why: The model is fitting noise in the training set that doesn't carry over to new data. Early stopping or regularisation helps.

questions.q: Why does a neural network need non-linear activation functions between its layers?
options: Otherwise the layers collapse into one linear map
They stop the weights from growing too large
They normalise each layer's outputs to mean zero
They make backpropagation run much faster on GPUs
questions.why: A composition of linear maps is still linear, so without a non-linearity like ReLU extra depth would add nothing.

questions.q: A disease affects 1% of patients. A model that always predicts 'healthy' scores 99% accuracy. Which number exposes how useless it is?
options: Its training loss
Its recall on the sick class
Its accuracy on the test set
Its accuracy on the healthy class
questions.why: It finds none of the sick patients, so recall on that class is 0, whatever the accuracy says.

questions.q: You raise a language model's sampling temperature from 0.2 to 1.5. What changes?
options: It becomes more factually accurate
It can read a much longer context
It generates tokens much faster
Its output gets more random
questions.why: Temperature divides the logits before softmax. Higher values flatten the distribution, so unlikely tokens get picked more often.

questions.q: You run k-nearest neighbours on two features, one in metres and one in grams, with very different ranges. What should you do first?
options: Scale the features to comparable ranges
Increase k until accuracy stops changing
Remove the feature with the larger range
Nothing: kNN ignores feature units
questions.why: kNN compares distances, so the feature with the biggest numbers dominates unless you standardise.

questions.q: A dataset has several X-ray images per patient. Why is a random image-level train/test split risky?
options: The test set will contain too few images
Random splits always change the class balance
X-rays must be split by file size
The same patient can land in both train and test
questions.why: The model can recognise the patient instead of the disease. Split by patient to measure performance on new people.

questions.q: In a very deep plain network, gradients shrink layer by layer until early layers barely learn. What did ResNet add to fix this?
options: Bigger convolution kernels in every layer
A higher learning rate for the early layers
Skip connections around each block
Dropout after every convolution layer
questions.why: Residual connections give gradients a direct path back through the network, so very deep models can train.

questions.q: Within a few steps your training loss explodes to NaN. What should you try first?
options: Lower the learning rate
Train for more epochs
Add more layers to the model
Remove the validation set
questions.why: Steps that are too large overshoot and blow up. A smaller learning rate (or gradient clipping) is the usual first fix.

questions.q: Which of these is an unsupervised learning task?
options: Predicting house prices from past sales
Grouping customers by their shopping habits
Classifying emails as spam or not spam
Detecting tumours in scans marked by doctors
questions.why: Clustering finds structure without labels. The others learn from labelled examples.

questions.q: What does dropout do during training?
options: Lowers the learning rate when loss plateaus
Removes the worst training examples
Randomly zeroes some activations at each step
Deletes layers that have small weights
questions.why: Each step trains a random sub-network, so units can't rely on each other. At test time dropout is switched off.

questions.q: What is a large language model like GPT trained to do during pre-training?
options: Classify sentences as true or false
Translate between pairs of languages
Predict the next token
Retrieve documents from a search index
questions.why: Pre-training is next-token prediction on a huge amount of text. Skills like answering questions emerge from that.

questions.q: In the update θ ← θ − η∇L(θ), what does η stand for?
options: The gradient of the loss
The learning rate
The model parameters
The loss value
questions.why: θ is the parameters, ∇L(θ) the gradient of the loss, and η the step size: the learning rate.

questions.q: Model A has higher precision than model B, but lower recall. What does that mean?
options: A must have a higher accuracy than B overall
A finds more positives, but raises more false alarms
A's alarms are more reliable, but A misses more
A must beat B at every possible threshold
questions.why: Precision is how often a positive prediction is right. Recall is how many of the real positives get found.

questions.q: Why do convolutional layers suit images better than fully connected layers?
options: They need no training data at all to work
They flatten the image into one long vector first
They are faster because they run only on GPUs
They reuse one small filter at every position
questions.why: Weight sharing and local connections cut the parameter count and let a pattern be detected anywhere in the image.

questions.q: Why keep a test set that is never used for training or tuning?
options: To make each training epoch run faster
To get an honest score on unseen data
To pick the best learning rate and epochs
To give the model more data to learn from
questions.why: Anything used to train or tune shapes your choices. Only untouched data shows how the model generalises.

questions.q: Which activation squashes any input into the range (0, 1)?
options: ReLU
Sigmoid
Tanh
Leaky ReLU
questions.why: Sigmoid maps to (0, 1), which is why it's used for binary probabilities. Tanh maps to (−1, 1); ReLU has no upper bound.

questions.q: A chatbot confidently cites a research paper that doesn't exist. What is this failure called?
options: Catastrophic forgetting
Mode collapse
Hallucination
Overfitting
questions.why: The model produces fluent text that isn't grounded in fact.

questions.q: One deep decision tree fits the training data perfectly but tests poorly. Which method trains many trees on bootstrap samples and averages them?
options: Gradient boosting
Logistic regression
Random forest
k-means
questions.why: Bagging many decorrelated trees averages away much of a single tree's variance. Boosting builds trees one after another instead.

questions.q: Why does early stopping count as a form of regularisation?
options: It reduces the number of layers in the model
It adds a penalty on large weights to the loss
It stops before the model fits noise
It removes noisy examples from the training set
questions.why: Validation loss usually bottoms out before training loss does. Stopping there limits how closely the model fits the training set.

questions.q: You fine-tune an ImageNet-pretrained model on just 500 labelled images of your own. Why does this beat training from scratch?
options: Pretrained models can't overfit small datasets
ImageNet already contains your 500 images
Fine-tuning doesn't need a learning rate
Its layers already detect edges and textures
questions.why: Transfer learning reuses general visual features, so the small dataset only has to teach the task-specific part.

questions.q: What does the gradient of a function at a point tell you?
options: The direction of steepest decrease
The direction of steepest increase
The function's average value
Where the function is smallest
questions.why: That's why gradient descent steps along the negative gradient: it's the direction of steepest decrease.

questions.q: What does a confusion matrix show for a classifier?
options: True classes against predicted classes
How the loss changed over each epoch of training
Which features the model relies on most
How similar the classes look to each other
questions.why: One axis is the true class, the other the predicted class. The diagonal holds the correct predictions.

questions.q: Which loss function is standard for multi-class classification?
options: Huber loss
Cross-entropy
Mean absolute error
Mean squared error
questions.why: Cross-entropy on softmax probabilities punishes confident wrong answers hard and gives good gradients. The other three are regression losses.

questions.q: Why do language models split text into pieces like 'un', 'believ', 'able' instead of whole words?
options: Shorter pieces make the model run much faster
Whole words can't be turned into vectors at all
Any new word can be built from known pieces
Subword pieces remove the need for embeddings
questions.why: Subword tokenizers like BPE keep the vocabulary small but still cover any word, including typos and new names.

questions.q: What does PCA find in a dataset?
options: The directions along which the data varies most
The cluster each point belongs to
The features most correlated with the label
The outliers furthest from the mean
questions.why: Principal components are orthogonal directions of maximum variance. Keeping the first few compresses the data with little loss.

questions.q: You standardise features with the mean and std of the whole dataset, then split it into train and test. What's wrong?
options: Standardisation only works on images
The model can no longer use the mean
Nothing: the order doesn't matter
Test-set statistics leaked into training
questions.why: Fit preprocessing on the training split only, then apply it to the test split. Otherwise the test set influences training.

questions.q: Compared with plain SGD, what does momentum add?
options: A running average of past gradients
A separate learning rate for every parameter
A penalty on large weights in the loss
Random noise added to each update
questions.why: Momentum keeps moving in consistent directions and damps zig-zagging, which speeds progress along narrow valleys.

questions.q: Which model's 2012 ImageNet win kick-started the deep learning boom in computer vision?
options: VGG
AlexNet
ResNet
LeNet
questions.why: AlexNet (Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton) cut the error sharply using GPUs, ReLU and dropout. LeNet came earlier; VGG and ResNet later.

questions.q: In PyTorch, why do you call optimizer.zero_grad() every training step?
options: It resets the weights to their initial values
It sets the learning rate to zero for warm-up
It clears gradients that would add up
It frees the model's GPU memory
questions.why: loss.backward() accumulates into .grad. Without clearing, each step would use the sum of all earlier gradients.

questions.q: Despite its name, what is logistic regression mostly used for?
options: Clustering
Classification
Predicting continuous values
Dimensionality reduction
questions.why: It models the probability of a class with a sigmoid, then thresholds that probability.

questions.q: What does a max-pooling layer do?
options: Adds the largest weight to each pixel
Doubles the feature map's resolution
Keeps each window's largest value
Averages all the pixels in the image
questions.why: It shrinks the feature map and makes the output less sensitive to small shifts.

questions.q: A classifier's ROC AUC is 0.5. What does that suggest?
options: It is right on exactly half of each class
Its probabilities are perfectly calibrated
It ranks no better than chance
It separates the classes perfectly
questions.why: AUC is the chance a random positive scores higher than a random negative. 0.5 is coin-flip ranking.

questions.q: What does batch normalisation do inside a network?
options: Normalises the input images once before training
Rescales the learning rate for each batch
Splits the data into equal-sized batches
Normalises a layer's activations over the mini-batch
questions.why: It standardises activations with batch statistics, then applies a learned scale and shift. Training gets faster and more stable.

questions.q: In self-attention, what decides how much one token attends to another?
options: Its query's dot product with the other token's key
How far apart the two tokens are
How common the other token is in the training data
The other token's value vector alone
questions.why: Scores are query·key (scaled), and a softmax turns them into weights over the values.

questions.q: Why does L1 regularisation tend to give sparse models, while L2 doesn't?
options: It punishes large weights much harder than L2 does
It drops low-variance features before training starts
Its pull doesn't fade as weights shrink, so they hit zero
It is applied only to the biases, never the weights
questions.why: The L1 penalty pulls with the same strength however small a weight gets, so weights reach exactly zero. L2's pull fades as weights shrink.

questions.q: Why are training images often flipped and cropped at random?
options: To add variety so the model generalises
To make the test set harder to score well on
To remove label noise from the dataset
To shrink the images so training runs faster
questions.why: Data augmentation creates new label-preserving views of each image, which reduces overfitting.

questions.q: In k-means clustering, what does k stand for?
options: The number of nearest neighbours
The number of features
The number of clusters
The number of iterations
questions.why: You choose k up front. The algorithm alternates between assigning points to the nearest centroid and moving each centroid to its points' mean.

questions.q: What does fine-tuning a pretrained language model mean?
options: Shrinking it by cutting out its last layers
Changing only the prompt, never the weights
Retraining it from scratch on new data
Training it further on task-specific data
questions.why: Fine-tuning starts from the pretrained weights and adapts them to your task with relatively little data.

questions.q: Which optimizer keeps running averages of both the gradients and their squares?
options: Plain SGD
RMSProp
SGD with momentum
Adam
questions.why: Adam combines momentum (the gradient average) with RMSProp-style scaling (the squared-gradient average). RMSProp keeps only the squares.

questions.q: You try 200 hyperparameter settings and report the best validation score as your result. Why is it likely too optimistic?
options: More settings always overfit the weights
Validation sets are always easier than test sets
Hyperparameters can't change validation scores
You picked it on the same data you're reporting
questions.why: The best of many noisy scores overfits the validation set. Report on a test set you didn't use for choosing.

questions.q: A GAN's generator starts producing nearly the same image whatever noise you feed it. What is this called?
options: Mode collapse
Overfitting
Label smoothing
Vanishing gradients
questions.why: The generator finds a few outputs that fool the discriminator and stops covering the variety of real data.

questions.q: Why call model.eval() before evaluating a model with dropout and batch norm?
options: So the weights are frozen and can't change any more
So dropout switches off and batch norm uses stored stats
So the model and its data move from GPU to CPU
So no gradients are computed, which saves memory
questions.why: eval() switches layer behaviour. Turning off gradient tracking is a separate job, done by torch.no_grad().

questions.q: In most ML papers, what does θ usually denote?
options: The model's parameters
The learning rate schedule
The training dataset
The value of the loss
questions.why: θ (theta) is the usual name for the weights being learned, as in L(θ).

questions.q: Which model predicts by following a series of yes/no questions about the features?
options: Linear regression
k-means
A support vector machine
A decision tree
questions.why: Each internal node tests a feature against a threshold. The leaf you land in gives the prediction.

questions.q: Which task means drawing a box around each object in an image and labelling it?
options: Image classification
Semantic segmentation
Image captioning
Object detection
questions.why: Classification gives one label per image, segmentation labels every pixel, and detection gives a box and a class per object.

questions.q: Your model scores poorly on both the training set and the validation set. What is the most likely problem?
options: The test set leaked into training
It is underfitting
It is overfitting the training data
The validation set is too large
questions.why: Overfitting shows a gap between training and validation. Poor scores on both mean the model hasn't captured the pattern yet.

questions.q: Self-attention on its own ignores word order. What do Transformers add so that order matters?
options: Layer normalisation
Positional encodings
A recurrent loop over the tokens
Larger embedding vectors
questions.why: Position information is added to (or rotated into) the token embeddings. Without it, shuffling the words wouldn't change what each token sees.

questions.q: Only 2% of your examples are fraud. Which is a sensible way to handle the imbalance?
options: Delete the fraud cases as outliers
Weight the fraud class more heavily in the loss
Copy the test set's fraud cases into training
Report accuracy, since it covers both classes
questions.why: Class weights (or resampling the training set) make mistakes on the rare class cost more. The test set must stay untouched.

questions.q: Why did ReLU largely replace sigmoid in the hidden layers of deep networks?
options: Its gradient doesn't vanish for positive inputs
It never outputs zero, so neurons can't die
Its outputs are probabilities between 0 and 1
It is smooth and differentiable at every point
questions.why: Sigmoid saturates, so gradients shrink at every layer. ReLU passes a gradient of 1 for positive inputs and is cheap to compute.

questions.q: Which metric suits a regression task like predicting house prices?
options: Area under the ROC curve
Mean absolute error
Macro F1 score
Average precision
questions.why: MAE (or RMSE) measures how far numeric predictions are from the truth. The other three are classification metrics.

questions.q: What is a word embedding?
options: A learned vector, close for similar words
A count of how often the word appears in text
A dictionary definition attached to each word
The index of the word's position in a sentence
questions.why: Embeddings like word2vec place words in a vector space where related meanings sit near each other.

questions.q: What is backpropagation?
options: Running the network backwards to generate inputs
Undoing the last weight update whenever the loss rises
Computing every weight's gradient with the chain rule
Feeding the network's outputs back in as new inputs
questions.why: It sends error signals from the output back through the layers, reusing intermediate results, so all gradients cost about one extra pass.

questions.q: What does softmax turn a vector of scores into?
options: Scores with mean 0 and variance 1
Positive numbers that sum to 1
A one-hot vector of the largest score
Values between −1 and 1
questions.why: softmax(z)ᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / Σⱼ exp(zⱼ): a probability distribution. Argmax would give the one-hot vector.

questions.q: Which encoder–decoder architecture, with skip connections between the two halves, is a classic for medical image segmentation?
options: ResNet-50
YOLO
U-Net
AlexNet
questions.why: U-Net's skip connections carry fine detail from the encoder to the decoder, so the masks keep sharp edges.

questions.q: What does a support vector machine try to maximise?
options: The variance of the projected data
Training accuracy at any cost
The margin between the classes
The number of support vectors
questions.why: It looks for the boundary with the widest gap to the nearest points of each class: the support vectors.

questions.q: Why is the training data usually shuffled before each epoch?
options: So the validation set changes every epoch
So the learning rate can stay fixed all along
So each example is seen twice per epoch
So batches don't follow the data's order
questions.why: If the data is sorted, say by class, consecutive batches would pull the weights one way at a time.

questions.q: A 'city' column holds values like 'Paris' and 'Tokyo'. What's a standard way to feed it to a linear model?
options: One-hot encode it
Drop it, since models need numbers
Replace each city with its alphabetical rank
Use the length of each city's name
questions.why: Ranks invent an order that isn't there. One-hot encoding gives each city its own column.

questions.q: What is an epoch?
options: One gradient update of the weights
One pass over all the training data
One mini-batch of training examples
Training one layer of the network
questions.why: An epoch is many steps: each step processes one mini-batch and makes one update.

questions.q: Who shared the 2018 Turing Award for deep learning with Yann LeCun and Yoshua Bengio?
options: Andrew Ng
Geoffrey Hinton
Demis Hassabis
Fei-Fei Li
questions.why: Hinton, LeCun and Bengio, often called the godfathers of deep learning, shared the ACM Turing Award for 2018.

questions.q: Why does a decoder-only model like GPT use a causal mask in attention?
options: So padding tokens are ignored
So attention only looks at nearby tokens
So a token can't attend to itself
So a token can't see the tokens after it
questions.why: In training it predicts every next token at once. The mask stops it peeking at the answer.

questions.q: Why use k-fold cross-validation instead of a single validation split?
options: It lets you train on the test set without any risk
It makes training k times faster than one split
It averages several splits, so the estimate is steadier
It removes the need to keep a separate test set
questions.why: Averaging over k different splits reduces the luck of any one split, especially on small datasets.

questions.q: What does IoU measure for a predicted bounding box?
options: Overlap area over the area of their union
The distance between the two boxes' centres
How confident the model is about that box
The share of the whole image the box covers
questions.why: Intersection over union is 1 for a perfect box and 0 for no overlap. Detection metrics count a hit above a threshold such as 0.5.

questions.q: How does gradient boosting build its ensemble?
options: One tree is grown, then pruned again and again
Each tree trains independently on a random sample
All trees vote and the majority wins
Each new tree fits the errors of the trees before it
questions.why: Boosting is sequential: every tree corrects what the ensemble still gets wrong. Random forests train their trees independently.

questions.q: What is a hyperparameter?
options: A new feature built from the raw input data
The model's output on the held-out test set
A setting you choose, like the learning rate
A weight the model learns by gradient descent
questions.why: Parameters are learned from data. Hyperparameters such as learning rate, depth and batch size are chosen by you, usually with a validation set.

questions.q: What do the filters in a CNN's first layer typically learn to detect?
options: The image's average brightness
Edges and colour blobs
Whole objects like faces and cars
The class label of the image
questions.why: Early layers find edges and textures; deeper layers combine them into parts and then objects.

questions.q: What does the variance of a probability distribution measure?
options: Which value is the most likely
The middle value once sorted
How spread out the values are
How lopsided its shape is
questions.why: Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean. Its square root is the standard deviation.

questions.q: What does RLHF use to improve a chatbot?
options: Hand-written grammar rules
A larger tokenizer vocabulary
More pre-training text from the internet
Human rankings of its answers
questions.why: Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a reward model on human rankings, then tunes the chatbot to score well on it.

questions.q: What does an autoencoder learn to do?
options: Sort inputs into a fixed set of labels
Write a short caption for each image
Compress its input and rebuild it
Predict the next item in a sequence
questions.why: The bottleneck forces it to keep the most important information. The code is useful for compression, denoising and anomaly detection.

questions.q: A model predicts whether a customer will cancel next month. One feature is 'date the account was closed'. What's the problem?
options: Its many unique values make the model underfit
Dates can never be used as model features
It has to be one-hot encoded before use
It's only known after the customer cancels
questions.why: This is target leakage: the feature is filled in because of the outcome, so it won't exist when you need the prediction.

questions.q: Why is Naive Bayes called 'naive'?
options: It ignores each class's prior probability
It can only ever handle two classes at once
It assumes features are independent per class
It needs no training data, only rules
questions.why: The independence assumption is rarely true, but it makes the model fast and often good enough, for spam filtering for example.

questions.q: What is a language model's context window?
options: The number of layers in the model
The set of websites it was trained on
The most tokens it can take in at once
The time it takes to answer
questions.why: Anything beyond the window is invisible to the model unless it is summarised or brought back in.

questions.q: Training crashes with a CUDA out-of-memory error. What is the quickest fix to try?
options: Add more layers
Increase the learning rate
Train for fewer epochs
Reduce the batch size
questions.why: Activation memory grows with batch size. Fewer epochs don't change peak memory at all.

questions.q: Your spam filter must almost never send a real email to spam. Which metric, for the spam class, matters most?
options: Precision
Recall
Mean squared error
Training accuracy
questions.why: Precision on spam asks: of the emails flagged as spam, how many really are? High precision means few real emails get flagged.

questions.q: What problem do LSTMs address compared with plain RNNs?
options: Learning without any labelled data
Remembering things over long sequences
Running fast on a CPU instead of a GPU
Processing images with many channels
questions.why: Gates control what the cell state keeps and forgets, so gradients survive across many time steps.

questions.q: What made Vision Transformers (ViT) different from CNNs?
options: They use much bigger convolution kernels
They work only on black-and-white images
They need no labelled training data at all
They run attention over image patches
questions.why: Each patch becomes a token, and attention lets any patch interact with any other from the first layer on.

questions.q: What is the bias–variance trade-off about?
options: Fairer models must always have higher error
Too simple misses patterns; too complex fits noise
Bigger datasets always need bigger learning rates
Bias terms add extra variance to a network's outputs
questions.why: Error splits into bias (wrong assumptions) and variance (sensitivity to the training sample). Model complexity trades one for the other.

questions.q: You predict tomorrow's sales from past data. Why is a random train/test split a bad idea?
options: Random splits always unbalance the classes
Time-series features can't be standardised
It trains on the future, tests on the past
There would be far too few days left to test
questions.why: With time series, split by time: train on earlier data and test on later data, as in real use.

questions.q: Which method classifies a point by the majority class among its closest training points?
options: k-nearest neighbours
k-means
Linear regression
Naive Bayes
questions.why: kNN stores the training set and votes among the k nearest points. k-means is a clustering method, despite the similar name.

questions.q: What does 'stride 2' mean for a convolution?
options: The filter is two pixels wide
The whole image is processed twice over
Two different filters run at each position
The filter moves two pixels at a time
questions.why: Skipping positions roughly halves the output size, a common way to downsample.

questions.q: What does weight decay do?
options: Stops training when validation loss rises
Lowers the learning rate a little each epoch
Removes the neurons whose weights are small
Shrinks weights toward zero each step
questions.why: It works like an L2 penalty: large weights cost something, which discourages overly complex fits.

questions.q: The 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer is known by which title?
options: Deep Residual Learning
Attention Is All You Need
Generative Adversarial Nets
Playing Atari with Deep RL
questions.why: Vaswani et al. replaced recurrence with self-attention, and nearly every modern LLM builds on it.

questions.q: BERT is pre-trained by hiding some words in each sentence. What must it do?
options: Predict the next word from the left side only
Translate the sentence into another language
Predict the hidden words from context on both sides
Say whether the sentence is positive or negative
questions.why: Masked language modelling lets BERT use context on both sides. GPT-style models only see the left.

questions.q: What does multi-head attention give over a single attention head?
options: Attention then runs in linear time in the length
Different heads can track different relations
It removes the need for positional information
Tokens can attend to the tokens that follow them
questions.why: Each head has its own query, key and value projections, so one can follow syntax while another follows, say, who 'it' refers to.

questions.q: When this model says 70%, it's right about 70% of the time, and the same holds at every confidence level. What property is that?
options: Regularisation
Recall
Robustness
Calibration
questions.why: A calibrated model's confidence matches its accuracy. Modern deep nets are often overconfident and need recalibrating.

questions.q: What is a validation set mainly used for?
options: Reporting the final score in a paper
Choosing hyperparameters and when to stop
Storing the examples the model got wrong
Training the model's weights a second time
questions.why: Training data fits the weights, validation data guides your choices, and the test set gives the final untouched estimate.

questions.q: Which family of models generates images by learning to remove noise step by step?
options: Diffusion models
Decision trees
Recurrent neural networks
Variational autoencoders
questions.why: A diffusion model learns to undo small amounts of added noise. Sampling runs that denoising from pure noise to an image.

questions.q: Linear regression is usually fit by minimising what?
options: The sum of squared errors
The cross-entropy of the labels
The number of misclassified points
The largest single error
questions.why: Ordinary least squares minimises squared residuals, and it even has a closed-form solution.

questions.q: What does the chain rule let you compute?
options: The mean of a probability distribution
The integral of a product of two functions
The inverse of a square matrix
The derivative of composed functions
questions.why: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x))·g′(x). Backpropagation is the chain rule applied layer by layer.

questions.q: What is the vanishing gradient problem?
options: The loss stops falling because the data runs out
Early layers get tiny gradients and barely learn
Too much dropout pushes all the weights to zero
Gradients grow until the weights become NaN
questions.why: Multiplying many small derivatives (like sigmoid's) makes them tiny. ReLU, good initialisation, normalisation and skip connections all help.

questions.q: Which of these is an encoder-only Transformer?
options: T5
BERT
GPT-2
LLaMA
questions.why: BERT reads its whole input with bidirectional attention. GPT-2 and LLaMA are decoder-only; T5 has an encoder and a decoder.

questions.q: You train with a batch size of 1 instead of 256. What tends to happen?
options: Each step needs more GPU memory
The model can no longer overfit
Gradients become exact, so fewer steps are needed
Gradients get noisier, but each step is cheap
questions.why: One example gives a rough estimate of the full gradient. Bigger batches average out the noise but cost more per step.

questions.q: What is 'zero-shot' use of a language model?
options: Using it before it has been trained
Running it with the temperature set to zero
Asking it a question it can't possibly answer
Giving a task with no worked examples
questions.why: Few-shot prompting includes a handful of solved examples; zero-shot gives only the instruction.

questions.q: What is the F1 score?
options: The plain average of accuracy and recall
The harmonic mean of precision and recall
The fraction of all predictions that are correct
The area under the precision–recall curve
questions.why: F1 is high only when both precision and recall are high. The fraction of correct predictions is accuracy.

questions.q: AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, was built by which lab?
options: IBM Research
DeepMind
OpenAI
Meta AI
questions.why: DeepMind's AlphaGo combined deep networks with Monte Carlo tree search and won the match 4–1.

questions.q: Why are a network's weights initialised randomly instead of all to zero?
options: All neurons in a layer would stay identical
Zero weights always make the loss come out as NaN
Zero weights would need a far larger learning rate
Random weights make every training run deterministic
questions.why: If all weights start equal, all neurons get the same gradient and stay identical. Randomness breaks the symmetry.

questions.q: Why are CNNs fairly robust to an object shifting a few pixels?
options: They share filters and pool over positions
Their first layer re-centres every object
They memorise every position in the training data
They are trained only on centred objects
questions.why: A feature detected in one place is detected anywhere, and pooling throws away some of the exact position.

questions.q: When a decision tree chooses a split, what is it trying to do?
options: Make each child as pure as possible
Put equal numbers of points in each child
Split on the feature with the largest values
Keep the tree as deep as possible
questions.why: Splits are chosen to cut impurity (Gini or entropy) the most.

questions.q: Some ages in your data are missing. Why might an extra 'age_missing' flag help?
options: It lets the model work out the missing ages exactly
Most models crash on any column that has gaps
It effectively doubles the amount of training data
The fact it's missing can itself be informative
questions.why: If missingness relates to the label (say, one kind of form skipped the field), the flag lets the model use that signal.

questions.q: What does a learning-rate schedule like cosine decay do?
options: Raises the learning rate as the loss falls
Lowers the learning rate gradually
Picks a random learning rate each epoch
Keeps the rate fixed but reshuffles the data
questions.why: Big steps early make fast progress; small steps late let the model settle into a good minimum.

questions.q: Which kind of model trains a generator and a discriminator against each other?
options: A Transformer
A GAN
A diffusion model
A VAE
questions.why: The generator tries to fool the discriminator, which tries to tell real images from generated ones.

questions.q: What are 'stop words' in classic NLP?
options: Punctuation-like words that mark a sentence's end
Words the model is never allowed to generate
Rare words replaced by an unknown-word token
Common words like 'the' and 'is', often dropped
questions.why: In bag-of-words models such words carry little signal, so they're often dropped. Modern Transformers usually keep them.

questions.q: A spam email gets P(spam) = 0.9. As that probability moves closer to 1, what happens to its cross-entropy loss?
options: It stays the same
It turns negative
It moves closer to 0
It moves closer to 1
questions.why: Cross-entropy is −log of the true class's probability, and −log 1 = 0.

questions.q: In attention, what is the job of the value vectors?
options: They hold the content that gets mixed
They decide which tokens attend to which
They store each token's position in the text
They normalise the attention scores to sum to 1
questions.why: Queries and keys produce the weights; the output is the weighted sum of the values.

questions.q: You lower a classifier's decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.2. What usually happens?
options: Recall goes up and precision goes down
Both precision and recall go up
Precision goes up and recall goes down
Nothing, since the model is unchanged
questions.why: More examples get called positive, so you catch more real positives but raise more false alarms.

questions.q: What does the kernel trick let an SVM do?
options: Separate many classes with one binary classifier
Train on unlabelled data by guessing the labels
Get curved boundaries without computing new features
Skip most of the training data to train faster
questions.why: A kernel computes dot products in a richer feature space directly, so the SVM gets non-linear boundaries cheaply.

questions.q: What is data leakage?
options: The model forgetting its older training data
Training on info you won't have at prediction time
Private training data being stolen from a server
Rows quietly going missing when a data file loads
questions.why: Leaks make validation scores look great and real-world performance poor.

questions.q: Which layer type gives a network memory of earlier inputs in a sequence?
options: A pooling layer
A batch-norm layer
A dropout layer
A recurrent layer
questions.why: An RNN passes a hidden state from each time step to the next.

questions.q: Which classic model learns word vectors by predicting a word's neighbours?
options: n-gram counts
TF-IDF
Word2Vec
Bag of words
questions.why: Word2Vec's skip-gram predicts surrounding words. TF-IDF and bag of words are counts, not learned vectors.

questions.q: Who coined the term 'machine learning' in 1959 while building a checkers-playing program?
options: John McCarthy
Marvin Minsky
Arthur Samuel
Alan Turing
questions.why: Samuel's checkers program improved by playing against itself. John McCarthy coined 'artificial intelligence'.

questions.q: Why is YOLO called a one-stage detector?
options: It detects only one object per image
It finds boxes and classes in one pass
It needs just one epoch of training
It uses just a single convolution layer
questions.why: Two-stage detectors like Faster R-CNN first propose regions and then classify them. YOLO does both at once, which makes it fast.

questions.q: What does gradient clipping protect against?
options: Exploding gradients
Vanishing gradients in the early layers
Slow data loading from disk
Overfitting to the training set
questions.why: If a gradient's norm passes a limit, it is scaled down. It's common when training RNNs and Transformers.

questions.q: What does KL divergence measure?
options: The straight-line distance between two points
How much one distribution differs from another
The linear correlation between two variables
The spread of a single probability distribution
questions.why: It's zero only when the two distributions match. It isn't symmetric, so it isn't a true distance.

questions.q: What does recall measure?
options: The share of positive predictions that are right
The share of all predictions that are right
The share of negatives the model gets right
The share of actual positives the model finds
questions.why: Recall = TP / (TP + FN). The other options describe precision, accuracy and specificity.

questions.q: What do the three channels of a typical colour image hold?
options: Brightness, contrast and sharpness
Three copies of the grey image
Width, height and depth
Red, green and blue intensities
questions.why: An RGB image is a height × width × 3 array of numbers.

questions.q: Why doesn't a language model know about events after its training data was collected?
options: Its tokenizer has no words for new events
It only knows what was in its training data
It forgets old facts as new ones happen
Its context window is too short
questions.why: Its knowledge stops at the training cutoff unless new information is put into the prompt.

questions.q: Which signal usually tells you to stop training early?
options: Training loss reaches exactly zero
Training accuracy passes 90% for the first time
Validation loss stops improving
The learning rate reaches its maximum
questions.why: Early stopping watches the validation metric with some patience and keeps the best checkpoint.

questions.q: Why is k-means usually run several times from different random starts?
options: Random starts help remove the outliers
It always needs three runs to converge
Each start tries out a different value of k
It can get stuck in a poor solution
questions.why: The result depends on the initial centroids. Running several times (or using k-means++) and keeping the best fit helps.

questions.q: How does a trained VAE generate a brand-new image?
options: Ask its discriminator to draw a new one
Run a training image through the encoder only
Decode a randomly sampled latent vector
Average two training images pixel by pixel
questions.why: Training pulls the latent space close to a simple Gaussian, so random samples decode to plausible images.

questions.q: What is a stratified split?
options: Every split keeps the same class proportions
Every image is cut into tiles before splitting
The hardest examples all go into the test split
Every split covers a different collection date
questions.why: With rare classes, a random split can leave a fold with almost none of them. Stratifying prevents that.

questions.q: Which symbol usually stands for the gradient?
options: ∂ (partial)
Σ (sigma)
Π (pi)
∇ (nabla)
questions.why: ∇f is the vector of partial derivatives ∂f/∂xᵢ. Σ is a sum and Π a product.

questions.q: Which method squeezes data into 2D for a plot while trying to keep similar points close?
options: Logistic regression
k-means
t-SNE
Gradient boosting
questions.why: t-SNE (like UMAP) is mainly for visualisation. Don't over-read the distances between far-apart clusters.

questions.q: What does a language model's tokenizer do?
options: Turns text into a list of integer IDs
Checks the text for spelling mistakes
Translates the text into English first
Removes any words the model hasn't seen before
questions.why: The model only sees token IDs, which are looked up in an embedding table.

questions.q: What happens to a 'dead' ReLU neuron?
options: Its weights become NaN
It outputs zero for every input and stops learning
It is removed from the network automatically
It outputs the same positive value for everything
questions.why: If its input is always negative, ReLU outputs 0 and passes no gradient. Leaky ReLU keeps a small slope to avoid this.

questions.q: Which metric is standard on object detection benchmarks like COCO?
options: Mean squared error
Top-5 classification accuracy
BLEU score
Mean average precision
questions.why: mAP averages precision over recall levels, classes and IoU thresholds. BLEU is a translation metric.

questions.q: CLIP was trained on image–caption pairs. How can it classify images into classes it never trained on?
options: By generating a brand-new label with a GAN
By running k-means clustering on the raw pixels
By memorising every class name found in ImageNet
By matching it to text like 'a photo of a dog'
questions.why: Images and text share one embedding space, and the class whose prompt lands closest to the image wins.

questions.q: What is learning-rate warm-up?
options: Raising the rate gradually over the first steps
Training a small model first, then the big one
Running a few epochs on the test data first
Starting with a high rate, then switching to Adam
questions.why: Early updates, with fresh optimizer statistics, can be wild, and warm-up keeps them small until things settle. It's standard for Transformers.

questions.q: Which of these is a regression problem?
options: Predicting tomorrow's temperature
Deciding whether an email is spam
Recognising a handwritten digit
Grouping news articles by topic
questions.why: Regression predicts a number. The others predict a category or find groups.

questions.q: Why are deep networks trained on GPUs?
options: They let models learn with far less data
They store more data than a hard drive
They do many matrix multiplications at once
They make models generalise better than CPUs
questions.why: Neural networks are mostly matrix multiplications, which a GPU spreads over thousands of cores at once.

questions.q: What did Alan Turing propose to judge whether a machine can think?
options: Whether it can beat a world chess champion
Whether it can pass for a human in chat
Whether it can solve maths problems faster
Whether it can store more facts than a person
questions.why: In 1950 Turing swapped 'can machines think?' for the imitation game, now called the Turing test.

questions.q: Which text representation counts how often each word appears, ignoring order?
options: Bag of words
Word2Vec
Positional encoding
Byte-pair encoding
questions.why: Bag of words loses word order: 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look identical.

questions.q: Adding more and more features to a linear model keeps raising training accuracy. Why can test accuracy fall?
options: It starts fitting noise in the extra features
The test set has its columns in a different order
Linear models break with more than ten features
Extra features slow testing more than training
questions.why: Each extra feature adds freedom, and with limited data some of it gets spent on chance patterns. Regularisation or feature selection helps.

questions.q: What is a 1×1 convolution mainly used for?
options: Blurring the image to remove noise
Detecting large shapes across the image
Changing the channel count cheaply
Doubling the image's height and width
questions.why: It mixes channels at each pixel without looking at neighbours. Inception and ResNet bottlenecks use it to shrink and expand channels.

questions.q: Events A and B are independent. What is P(A and B)?
options: P(A) × P(B)
P(A) − P(B)
P(A) / P(B)
P(A) + P(B)
questions.why: Independence means knowing A tells you nothing about B, so the joint probability factorises.

questions.q: Which curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across thresholds?
options: The learning curve
The precision–recall curve
The ROC curve
The loss curve
questions.why: Each threshold gives one (FPR, TPR) point, and the area under the curve is ROC AUC.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a loss function?
options: To remove bad examples from the data
To choose the learning rate for each step
To score how wrong the predictions are
To decide how many layers the model needs
questions.why: Training adjusts the weights to make this number smaller.

questions.q: The original Transformer, built for translation, has which two parts?
options: A policy and a value network
A tokenizer and a classifier
A generator and a discriminator
An encoder and a decoder
questions.why: The encoder builds representations of the source sentence. The decoder writes the translation while attending to them.

questions.q: Going deeper into a typical CNN, what happens to the feature maps' spatial size and channel count?
options: Both grow
The size grows while the channels shrink
Both stay the same
The size shrinks while the channels grow
questions.why: Downsampling trades resolution for more and richer feature maps: ResNet-50 goes from 224×224×3 to 7×7×2048.

questions.q: How does layer normalisation differ from batch normalisation?
options: It normalises each example on its own
It normalises only the network's input layer
It normalises the whole dataset once before training
It only runs during evaluation, not training
questions.why: LayerNorm doesn't depend on the batch, so it behaves the same at any batch size. That's why Transformers use it.

questions.q: What is the curse of dimensionality?
options: In many dimensions, data is sparse and distances blur
High-resolution images need far more GPU memory
Accuracy always drops when there are many classes
Deep networks with many layers take far longer to train
questions.why: The space grows exponentially, so you need far more data, and near and far neighbours end up at similar distances.

questions.q: Why remove near-duplicate images before splitting into train and test?
options: Duplicates make the whole dataset slower to load
Models can't train on two identical images
Copies across the split inflate the test score
Duplicates lower the resolution of the images
questions.why: The model would be graded on images it has, in effect, already seen.

questions.q: What does ŷ (y-hat) usually mean?
options: The model's prediction
The true label
The average label
The label's variance
questions.why: y is the ground truth and ŷ the estimate. A loss compares the two.

questions.q: What does an embedding layer do?
options: Maps each ID to a learned vector
Joins two separate networks together
Adds random noise to the inputs
Compresses images into smaller files
questions.why: It's a trainable table: row i is the vector for item i, learned along with the rest of the network.

questions.q: Who led the creation of ImageNet, the dataset that drove a decade of vision research?
options: Andrej Karpathy
Ian Goodfellow
Andrew Ng
Fei-Fei Li
questions.why: Fei-Fei Li led ImageNet, and its yearly challenge is where AlexNet broke through. Ian Goodfellow invented GANs.

questions.q: Which architecture made deep stacks of small 3×3 convolutions popular, at 16 to 19 layers?
options: AlexNet
VGG
YOLO
U-Net
questions.why: VGG showed that depth with small filters works well: two 3×3 convs see as much as one 5×5 with fewer weights.

questions.q: Why does self-attention get expensive on very long inputs?
options: Attention needs a separate copy of the weights per token
Every token scores every other token: n² pairs
Each extra token adds a new layer to the model
Attention scores are squared before the softmax
questions.why: n tokens make n × n scores, so doubling the context quadruples attention's cost. Many efficient-attention methods attack this.

questions.q: Early in training, with heavy dropout and augmentation, training accuracy sits below validation accuracy. Why?
options: The validation set has leaked into the training set
The model is already overfitting the training set
Dropout and augmentation only handicap training
Validation is run with a higher learning rate
questions.why: The training score comes from a handicapped model on harder inputs. At evaluation, dropout is off and the images are clean.

questions.q: In logistic regression, what does the sigmoid of w·x + b give you?
options: The predicted probability of the positive class
The variance of the prediction
The distance from x to the nearest training point
The number of errors on the training set
questions.why: The linear score is a log-odds, and the sigmoid turns it into a probability between 0 and 1.

questions.title: Midnight Classification
questions.q: You are training logistic regression to predict whether a shop is busy. It is busy at 23:00, 00:00, and 01:00, but quiet at other hours. Which representation lets logistic regression express this exact pattern with a linear decision boundary?
options: Raw hour as an integer from 0 to 23
Hour standardized to mean 0 and variance 1
sin(2πh/24) and cos(2πh/24)
Squared hour h²
questions.why: On the unit circle, the three busy hours are adjacent and can be separated from all other integer hours by a linear threshold on cosine.

questions.title: The Time Zone Trap
questions.q: You are predicting when people sleep using data from 20 countries. Sleep patterns depend primarily on local hour, but timestamps are stored in UTC. Which preprocessing most directly represents this pattern?
options: Convert timestamps to local time, then make cyclic hour features
Standardize UTC hour
Remove the time zone and retain UTC hour unchanged
Convert timestamps to Unix seconds
questions.why: Local time aligns the human activity pattern across countries; cyclic encoding handles midnight adjacency.

questions.title: The Surprisingly Accurate Medical Model
questions.q: A dataset contains 10 images from each patient. A random image split gives 97% accuracy, but deployment will involve entirely new patients. Which validation split best estimates deployment performance?
options: Stratify individual images by diagnosis
Increase validation fraction from 20% to 40%
Shuffle images more thoroughly
Put all images from each patient into only one split
questions.why: A patient group split prevents identity and correlated imaging conditions leaking between training and validation.

questions.title: Predicting Tomorrow
questions.q: You predict electricity consumption at 14:00 tomorrow from past hourly consumption. Which candidate feature uses unavailable future information?
options: Consumption at 14:00 yesterday
A centered moving average around tomorrow at 14:00
Average consumption over the previous seven days
The hour of day
questions.why: A centered window around the forecast time contains tomorrow's target and later values.

questions.title: The Perfect Identifier
questions.q: A categorical device_id is nearly unique per row. You replace IDs with their average target computed on all training rows, and a classifier gets 100% training accuracy but chance validation accuracy. Which change most directly prevents this encoding from giving each training row its own label?
options: Use labels from other folds to encode each training row
Increase the number of epochs
Standardize encoded values
Add raw device_id as a numerical feature
questions.why: Out of fold target encoding prevents a row's own label from entering its encoded input.

questions.title: Missing Values as Information
questions.q: A lab sensor sometimes returns NaN. Whether a value is missing remains predictive of the label even after accounting for all observed values. What should you add?
options: Impute zero and do nothing else
Discard every incomplete row
Impute and add a binary missingness indicator
Replace every value with its rank
questions.why: A missingness flag preserves the information in the observation process itself.

questions.title: PCA’s Hidden Failure
questions.q: You have independent features x₁ (variance 100, unrelated to the label) and x₂ (variance 0.01, perfectly determines the label). You apply unstandardized PCA and retain one component. In the population limit, what is retained?
options: x₂, because PCA is label aware
x₁, losing the label information
An equal mixture of x₁ and x₂
Whichever has greater mutual information with the label
questions.why: PCA is unsupervised and prioritizes variance, not predictive relevance.

questions.title: A Distance Problem
questions.q: You train KNN with two equally relevant measurements. One numerical column has values around 1; the other has values around 10,000 solely because of its units. You use Euclidean distance. What is the most appropriate first change?
options: Increase k until the unit difference disappears
Apply PCA without scaling
Switch to a regression estimator
Scale features using statistics fitted only on training data
questions.why: Raw Euclidean distance is sensitive to feature units; training only scaling avoids validation leakage.

questions.title: The Miraculous Image Validation
questions.q: You create five crops of every labeled photograph, then randomly split the crops into train and validation. The validation score jumps sharply. What is the cleanest correction?
options: Split the original photographs first, then augment the training originals
Apply more aggressive augmentation to validation crops
Use a larger validation fraction after augmentation
Keep the split and add dropout
questions.why: Crops from one photograph are highly correlated; split at the source image level before augmentation.

questions.title: A Category That Has Never Appeared
questions.q: A model uses one hot encoded country codes. At inference, a previously unseen country appears. Which pipeline is robust without learning preprocessing from validation or test labels?
options: Refit the encoder on the test set alone
Assign the new country the label of the most common training country
Fit the encoder on training data with unknown categories ignored during transform
Replace all country names by their alphabetical positions
questions.why: An encoder fit on training categories with explicit unknown category handling keeps the feature space stable.

questions.title: AUC Without Better Predictions
questions.q: A binary model outputs distinct real valued scores. You replace every score s with sigmoid(5s). In exact arithmetic, what is guaranteed?
options: ROC AUC increases but log loss stays fixed
ROC AUC is unchanged; probability calibration may change
ROC AUC and log loss are both unchanged
ROC AUC decreases because sigmoid compresses large scores
questions.why: A strictly increasing function preserves all score rankings, so it preserves binary ROC AUC but not probability values.

questions.title: The Rare Disease Shift
questions.q: A classifier has unchanged true positive rate and false positive rate in two populations. The disease becomes much rarer, and both rates are strictly between 0 and 1. What happens to precision?
options: It must increase
It stays unchanged because recall stayed unchanged
It equals the false positive rate
It decreases
questions.why: With a lower positive base rate, false positives occupy a larger share of predicted positives.

questions.title: The 95% Accuracy Trap
questions.q: A test set has 95 negative and 5 positive examples. Model A predicts every example negative. Model B gets 4 positives right, misses 1 positive, and wrongly flags 6 negatives. Which has the higher positive class F1?
options: Model A, because its accuracy is higher
Both have F1 = 0.5
Model B, even though its accuracy is lower
Both have equal F1 because the test set is fixed
questions.why: Model A has positive F1 = 0; Model B has F1 = 2·4/(2·4+6+1) = 8/15.

questions.title: The Batch Metric Bug
questions.q: You report test set F1 by computing F1 separately for each minibatch and averaging the batch F1 values. Batches have different class proportions. What computes the true F1 of the complete test set?
options: Take the median batch F1
Concatenate all predictions and targets, then compute F1 once
Weight each batch F1 by the number of examples
Use the mean batch F1 only if batch size is constant
questions.why: F1 is a nonlinear function of total TP, FP, and FN; averaging batch F1 generally gives a different result.

questions.title: The Best of 100 Models
questions.q: You train 100 configurations and pick the one with highest accuracy on one fixed validation set. The winning validation score is unusually high. What is the main statistical concern?
options: The model always has too many parameters
Using a fixed validation set causes training gradients to vanish
Validation accuracy is always an underestimate
Selecting the maximum over noisy validation estimates gives an optimistic winning score
questions.why: Trying many configurations can overfit the validation set even without directly training on its labels.

questions.title: The Overconfident Group
questions.q: Among 1,000 examples receiving predicted probability 0.8, only 500 are actually positive. What can you directly conclude about calibration for this group?
options: The model is overconfident at 0.8
The model has ROC AUC = 0.5
The classifier has recall 50%
The model is underconfident at 0.8
questions.why: For calibrated 0.8 predictions, approximately 80% should be positive; only 50% are.

questions.title: Expensive False Negatives
questions.q: A calibrated model outputs P(y=1|x)=p. A false positive costs 1 unit, a false negative costs 100 units, and correct decisions cost 0. With no other constraints, when should you predict positive?
options: When p > 0.5
When p > 1/101
Only when p = 1
questions.why: Predict positive when expected FP cost 1−p is less than expected FN cost 100p, hence p > 1/101.

questions.title: Lowering the Threshold
questions.q: For a fixed set of binary classifier scores, you lower the threshold used to predict positive. Which statement is guaranteed, assuming the positive class is present?
options: Recall cannot decrease
Precision must decrease
Accuracy must increase
F1 must increase
questions.why: Lowering the threshold never turns a predicted positive into negative, so the number of true positives cannot fall.

questions.title: The Log Transform That Does Nothing
questions.q: You fit an exact greedy decision tree using all candidate threshold partitions. Every value of one positive numerical feature is replaced by its logarithm, which preserves their strict order. What is true about the possible splits on that feature?
options: The best split must move to a different subset
No threshold split is possible after logging
The feature must become less useful
The same training subsets remain achievable by thresholds
questions.why: Strict monotonic transforms preserve ordering; a decision tree threshold still separates the same subsets.

questions.title: XOR with Logistic Regression
questions.q: Two binary inputs x₁ and x₂ have label 1 exactly when one, but not both, is 1. Ordinary logistic regression cannot classify all four possible pairs perfectly. Which extra feature makes linear separation possible?
options: x₁ + x₂
x₁ − x₂
x₁·x₂
A constant bias feature
questions.why: An interaction term permits a decision rule based on x₁+x₂−2x₁x₂, which is 1 only when the inputs differ.

questions.title: Two Rings
questions.q: Unlabeled 2D points form two thin concentric rings separated by a clear empty gap. Which method is naturally suited to recover the two ring shaped clusters?
options: DBSCAN with suitable parameters
Standard KMeans with k=2
One principal component followed by KMeans
A linear separator
questions.why: Density based clustering can identify nonconvex connected regions separated by empty space; centroid methods favor convex groups.

questions.title: One Thousand Copies of the Same Tree
questions.q: You ensemble 1,000 trees. Each tree is identical, trained on the same data, and makes exactly the same predictions. What is the main limitation?
options: Voting reduces errors by a factor of 1,000
Their mistakes are perfectly correlated, so averaging gives no improvement
Ensembling identical models changes the decision boundary dramatically
Identical trees cannot be combined by majority voting
questions.why: If every model outputs the same value, their average and vote equal one tree's output.

questions.title: Units Change the Regularized Model
questions.q: A logistic regression model uses L2 regularization with a fixed penalty coefficient. You convert one input feature from meters to millimeters and retrain without rescaling features. Why might predictions change?
options: Logistic regression cannot accept values above 100
Conversion changes which labels are positive
The L2 penalty acts on coefficients and is not invariant to rescaling one feature
All sigmoid activations become zero on large inputs
questions.why: The coefficient compensates for units, but its squared penalty changes relative to other coefficients.

questions.title: Duplicating a Neighbor
questions.q: For a test point, the three nearest training examples are (distance 0.1, class 1), (0.2, class 0), and (0.3, class 0). A 3NN classifier predicts 0. You add an exact duplicate of the first training example. What does 3NN now predict?
options: Class 1
Class 0
An error because identical points are forbidden
The prediction remains unchanged by definition
questions.why: The three nearest are now two class 1 examples at 0.1 and one class 0 example at 0.2.

questions.title: Which Penalty Can Discard a Feature?
questions.q: You want a linear model to perform feature selection by making some learned coefficients exactly zero. Which penalty is specifically associated with this sparse behavior?
options: An L2 penalty only
An L1 penalty
Neither L1 nor L2 can produce zero coefficients
Increasing batch size
questions.why: L1's nonsmooth penalty at zero encourages exact zeros; L2 typically shrinks coefficients continuously.

questions.title: The Invisible Batch Matrix
questions.q: In PyTorch, predictions have shape (B, 1) and regression labels have shape (B,), with B>1. You pass both directly to nn.MSELoss. What happens?
options: PyTorch always raises a hard shape error
PyTorch silently reshapes labels to (B,1) before the loss
The arrays broadcast to (B,B), producing a wrong pairwise loss (typically with a warning)
The loss uses only the first prediction
questions.why: Broadcasting aligns trailing dimensions, expanding (B,1) and (B,) to (B,B).

questions.title: Four Steps, One Update
questions.q: You accumulate gradients from four equally sized minibatches and take one SGD step. Loss on each minibatch is its mean. Assume no batch dependent layers or other stochastic effects. What is needed to match the full batch mean gradient?
options: Divide each minibatch loss by 4 before backward
Multiply each loss by 4
Call optimizer.step() after every backward
Set every gradient to zero between minibatches
questions.why: Each minibatch mean must contribute one quarter to the average gradient over four equal minibatches.

questions.title: Why Accumulation Is Not Quite a Large Batch
questions.q: You accumulate gradients over four minibatches instead of processing one large batch. Loss scaling is correct, but results still differ when the model uses BatchNorm in training mode. Why?
options: The optimizer is unable to add gradients
The learning rate is automatically divided by four
BatchNorm disables backpropagation during accumulation
BatchNorm computes normalization statistics separately on each small minibatch
questions.why: Gradient accumulation cannot reproduce large batch BatchNorm statistics merely by rescaling losses.

questions.title: A Head That Never Trains
questions.q: You create an optimizer, then replace model.fc with a new nn.Linear layer. The new parameters have requires_grad=True and receive gradients, but they never update. What is the most likely reason?
options: The backbone is in eval mode
The optimizer does not contain the newly created layer's parameters
A new nn.Linear cannot be trained by SGD
requires_grad=True prevents optimizer updates
questions.why: Optimizers retain parameter references from construction time and do not automatically discover replacement layers.

questions.title: Frozen But Still Changing
questions.q: You set requires_grad=False on every parameter of a pretrained BatchNorm backbone, but leave model.train() active while training a new head. Which backbone state can still change?
options: The frozen convolution weights
The frozen BatchNorm affine gamma parameters
BatchNorm running mean and running variance
All requires_grad=False parameters
questions.why: BatchNorm running statistics are buffers that update in training mode even when its parameters are frozen.

questions.title: Two Inference Switches
questions.q: You want standard Dropout disabled, BatchNorm to use stored statistics, and PyTorch not to construct an autograd graph for inference. Which combination achieves all three?
options: model.eval() and torch.no_grad()
model.eval() alone
torch.no_grad() alone
optimizer.zero_grad() and model.train()
questions.why: eval controls module behavior, while no_grad separately disables gradient recording.

questions.title: A Confident Numerical Disaster
questions.q: A binary classifier produces an extremely negative logit for a positive label. You want to compute stable binary cross entropy directly from logits. Which PyTorch option is designed for this?
options: torch.nn.MSELoss on logits
sigmoid followed by torch.log manually
torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss applied to a single logit
torch.nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss on the raw logits
questions.why: BCEWithLogitsLoss combines sigmoid and the loss in a numerically stable computation.

questions.title: Two Independent Lookups
questions.q: One attention layer must retrieve a color description from one token and a position description from a different token, with independently chosen attention weights. Which design most directly provides two separate attention distributions?
options: Increase only the value dimension of a single head
Use two attention heads with separately learned queries and keys
Remove the softmax from one head
Apply the same attention weights twice
questions.why: Each head can learn its own query/key attention matrix, unlike a single softmax shared across all value channels.

questions.title: Patch Order Without Position
questions.q: A Transformer image classifier has a fixed CLS token, tokenwise operations, full self attention, and no positional information. At inference, you permute all patch tokens but leave CLS in place. What happens to the final CLS embedding?
options: It stays identical in exact arithmetic
It becomes a corresponding permutation of itself
It necessarily changes because attention is order sensitive
All attention probabilities become uniform
questions.why: Without positional information, permuting patch inputs only permutes patch outputs; the fixed CLS output is invariant.

questions.title: A Smaller Patch, a Larger Bill
questions.q: A vision Transformer processes 224×224 images with nonoverlapping 16×16 patches. You change the patch size to 8×8. Ignoring CLS and other special tokens, how does the number of patch to patch attention scores change?
questions.why: Patch count grows from 14²=196 to 28²=784 (4×); pairwise attention scores grow by 4²=16×.

questions.title: The Cheating Language Model
questions.q: An autoregressive language model gets nearly perfect training next token accuracy but fails at generating text. You discover that during training each position could attend to later positions containing target tokens. What should have prevented this?
options: Layer normalization
A larger vocabulary
Dropout on the output head
A causal attention mask
questions.why: Causal masking blocks access to future tokens, preserving the intended next token prediction task.

questions.title: Segmentation Masks That Invent Classes
questions.q: You resize a semantic segmentation image and its integer class mask. After resizing, the mask contains values between class IDs that never existed originally. What is the likely error?
options: You used nearest neighbor interpolation for the mask
You used bilinear interpolation for the class mask instead of nearest neighbor
You normalized RGB channels
You set the image size to a multiple of 32
questions.why: Bilinear interpolation blends class IDs; nearest neighbor interpolation preserves discrete labels.

questions.title: The Flipped Bounding Box
questions.q: An image uses continuous horizontal coordinates from 0 to W=100. A bounding box spans x₁=10 to x₂=30. You flip the image horizontally. What should its new horizontal bounds be?
questions.why: Under a horizontal flip x becomes W−x, so (x₁,x₂) maps to (W−x₂,W−x₁).

questions.title: A Nearly Perfect Segmenter
questions.q: Exactly 98% of pixels in a test image are background and 2% are foreground objects. A model predicts every pixel as background. Which statement is correct?
options: Pixel accuracy is 98%, but foreground IoU is 0
Pixel accuracy is 100% because background dominates
Foreground IoU is 98%
Foreground recall is 98%
questions.why: All background pixels are correct, but no foreground pixel is correctly predicted.

questions.title: An Augmentation That Lies
questions.q: You classify cropped handwritten digits, including 6 and 9. Some rotations turn a valid 6 into an apparent 9, but the augmentation preserves the original label. What is the risk?
options: Rotation never affects digit identity
It only changes the normalization statistics
It guarantees invariance and higher accuracy
It creates contradictory labels, potentially hurting learning
questions.why: Not every image transformation preserves the semantic label; label violating augmentation introduces supervision noise.

questions.title: Same Words, Different Meaning
questions.q: A classifier using only unordered word counts receives "the cat chased the dog" and "the dog chased the cat". The intended labels differ according to who chased whom. What is its fundamental limitation?
options: It cannot count the total number of words
Unigram counts discard word order, so both inputs have the same representation
It lacks enough training epochs
It cannot process repeated words
questions.why: Bag of words is invariant to token permutations; ngrams or an order aware encoder can preserve the distinction.

questions.title: Short Texts Look Small
questions.q: A text encoder pads every sequence to 128 tokens with zero padding vectors, then simply averages all 128 embeddings. Short documents produce much smaller average vector magnitudes than long ones. What is the most direct correction?
options: Add more padding tokens
Train a larger tokenizer vocabulary
Average only over real tokens using a padding mask
Sort all tokens alphabetically before pooling
questions.why: Masked pooling divides the sum by the actual number of real tokens, not the padded length.

questions.title: The Resampling Shortcut
questions.q: An audio clip contains 16,000 PCM samples captured at 16,000 samples per second. A model expects 8,000 samples per second. You change only the sample rate metadata to 8,000, leaving the sample array unchanged. What happens on playback?
options: Duration stays 1 second and pitch stays the same
Duration stays 1 second but pitch doubles
Duration halves to 0.5 seconds
Duration becomes 2 seconds and pitch is halved
questions.why: 16,000 samples at 8,000 samples/second play for two seconds; correct resampling changes the sample data.

questions.title: The Crop That Removes the Label
questions.q: In a binary vision task, y=1 means the target object is visible somewhere in the image. You crop a positive image so the object is completely excluded, but keep y=1. What is wrong?
options: The crop is now mislabeled for the stated task
Cropping positive images can never be used
The crop becomes a valid positive because the original image was positive
Only the learning rate must change
questions.why: An augmentation that removes the target object violates the labeling rule unless the label is updated.

questions.title: The Speaker and the Room
questions.q: You recognize known speakers from short audio clips. Every recording session contains many clips, and room acoustics stay constant within a session. Deployment will use new sessions in new rooms. Which validation design is most revealing, assuming each speaker has recordings in multiple rooms?
options: Randomly split individual frames from every clip
Hold out whole sessions and rooms while keeping the speakers represented in training
Randomly split clips from the same sessions
Duplicate rare speakers' clips before making a random split
questions.why: Whole session and room holdouts test speaker identity rather than memorizing recording conditions.

questions.title: Can You Tell Train from Test?
questions.q: You label training rows 0 and test rows 1, use features only, and train a classifier to tell them apart. Its cross-validated ROC AUC is 0.97. What does this most directly indicate?
options: Train and test differ in distribution, so random validation may mislead
The features are strongly predictive of the original task labels
Test labels have leaked into the training data through shared features
The classifier has overfit, so its cross-validated AUC carries no meaning
questions.why: A classifier that separates train from test exposes covariate shift, so a validation set drawn randomly from train will not mimic test conditions.

questions.title: Filling Holes with the Mean
questions.q: A feature has variance 4. At random, 30% of its values go missing, independently of everything else. You replace each missing value with the mean of the observed ones. Roughly what is the feature's variance afterwards?
options: About 4.0
About 2.8
About 2.0
About 1.2
questions.why: Imputed entries add no squared deviation but still count in n, so the variance shrinks to about 0.7 × 4 = 2.8.

questions.title: Balanced Training, Rare Reality
questions.q: To train faster you discard negatives until 50% of the training rows are positive, while only 1% of real cases are. The model, calibrated on the balanced data, outputs 0.80 for a new case. Assuming only class proportions differ, what is its true probability of being positive?
options: About 0.01
About 0.04
About 0.40
About 0.80
questions.why: Undersampling inflates the odds, so multiply by the real prior odds 0.01/0.99 (balanced prior odds are 1): 4 × 0.0101 ≈ 0.04 odds, hence p ≈ 0.04.

questions.title: The Hidden Ceiling
questions.q: In a binary test set, 10% of the labels are flipped at random, independently of the inputs. A model has 90% accuracy against the clean labels. What accuracy does it measure against the noisy labels?
questions.why: It agrees with a noisy label when it is right and the label intact (0.9 × 0.9) or wrong and the label flipped (0.1 × 0.1): 0.82.

questions.title: A Chance Baseline
questions.q: Only 2% of examples are positive. A model assigns scores that are random and unrelated to the label. What are its expected ROC AUC and average precision (area under the precision-recall curve)?
options: ROC AUC 0.5 and average precision 0.5
ROC AUC 0.02 and average precision 0.02
ROC AUC 0.98 and average precision 0.02
ROC AUC 0.5 and average precision 0.02
questions.why: Random scores give AUC 0.5, but precision at every recall level equals the 2% positive rate, so average precision is about 0.02.

questions.title: Accurate but Overconfident
questions.q: A balanced binary classifier has 85% validation accuracy and a validation log loss of 0.80 nats. A model that always outputs probability 0.5 scores ln 2 ≈ 0.69. What does the comparison show?
options: Its probabilities are worse than constant ones, from confident errors
It must beat the constant model, since accuracy is far above 50%
The log loss must be a bug, since it cannot exceed ln 2
Log loss and accuracy always rank models in exactly the same order
questions.why: Log loss punishes confident mistakes without bound, so an accurate model can still assign worse probabilities than a model that always says 0.5.

questions.title: The Step That Is Too Long
questions.q: You minimise f(w) = 5w² (second derivative 10) with plain gradient descent from w = 1. Which fixed learning rate makes the iterates diverge?
questions.why: Each step multiplies w by 1 − 10·lr, which exceeds magnitude 1 only when lr > 0.2: 0.25 gives −1.5, while 0.15 gives −0.5 and still converges.

questions.title: Points That Do Not Matter
questions.q: You fit a linear soft-margin SVM, then delete one training point that is correctly classified and lies well outside the margin, and refit. What happens to the hyperplane?
options: It shifts slightly toward the class of the deleted point
